newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives take heart from poll.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives take heart from poll.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's embattled Conservatives believe the election campaign could be turning their way after an opinion poll on Thursday showed a dramatic narrowing of the opposition Labour Party's lead.
After weeks of struggling in Labour's wake, the Conservatives found themselves, according to a MORI poll in The Times newspaper, just 15 points adrift compared with 27 points last week.

Major's aides said he believed the campaign for the May 1 general election was now beginng to come alive, with the focus turning to more substantive issues rather than "sleaze" stories about his party.

The Conservatives were also able to take comfort from a Gallup poll for Channel 4 television news which showed that despite Labour's huge poll lead, 50 percent of voters are not firmly committed to voting for one party or another.
The poll gave Labour 54 percent, the Conservatives 31 percent and the minority Liberal Democrats 10 percent.
But another poll showed Labour edging even further ahead despite its policy reversals and contradictory attitudes to privatising state assets.
A Gallup poll for Thursday's Daily Telegraph gave Labour 53 percent, the Conservatives 30 percent and the Liberal Democrats 11 percent.
Labour's lead had widened to 23 points from 19 points on Wednesday.
"Key to the Tories' (Conservatives') inability to make consistent inroads on the Labour lead is the issue of trust," the Telegraph newspaper said.
"Attempts by the Tories to show the Labour Party are shifting their ground on policy issues such as privatisation seem to be backfiring."

Attempts by the Conservatives to switch attention away from "sleaze" have been sabotaged by the emergence of veteran BBC war correspondent Martin Bell to fight the Tatton constituency against former government minister Neil Hamilton, who denies allegations he took cash in return for asking questions in parliament.
Labour agreed on Wednesday evening it would not field a candidate in Tatton, provided the Liberal Democrats did the same, in order to give Bell a clear run against Hamilton.
Labour leader Tony Blair had earlier stepped up his criticism of Major for standing by Hamilton.

At an election rally of Labour supporters in Plymouth, western England, Blair blasted Major for showing weak leadership in not dumping Hamilton, even though the Tatton MP had admitted breaking parliamentary rules by failing to declare gifts and payments.
Hamilton strenuously denies the more serious charge that he accepted bundles of cash from Mohammed al Fayed, owner of London department store Harrods, in return for asking questions in parliament.
